title: cfd solver
tag: a computational fluid dynamics mini-solver made in js
description: a high-performance Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) fluid dynamics solver built for the web, simulates real-time fluid structure
techSpecs: engineered a custom lattice boltzmann method (lbm) solver. i utilized float32array typed arrays to bypass javascript performance bottlenecks, enabling stable 60fps fluid simulation within the html5 canvas.
why: i wanted a lightweight way to experiment with fluid dynamics without spinning up heavy desktop cfd packages. being able to drop obstacles or flexible beams into a flow field and watch vortices form in real time felt like the perfect interactive learning tool.
learned: i got a much deeper appreciation for the lattice boltzmann approach versus traditional navier-stokes solvers—how the discrete velocity sets and collision/streaming steps work, and how to couple fluid pressure/velocity fields back to structural deformation for simple fsi. web workers and glsl shader tricks for keeping the simulation interactive were also new territory for me.
challenges: stability at higher reynolds numbers and preventing numerical blow-ups when the flexible structure moved a lot were constant headaches. performance in pure javascript before offloading more work to the gpu was limiting, and getting the fluid-structure coupling stable without introducing artificial damping or energy loss took a lot of iteration. the project is still marked in-progress for a reason.

title: fea generative cto engine
tag: custom physics engine that strips away material to find the ultimate structural shape
description: built a 2D generative design engine from scratch to figure out how the math behind aerospace lightweighting actually works
techSpecs: architected a generative solver for structural lightweighting. i optimized the global stiffness matrix assembly using scipy sparse matrices to efficiently handle topologies.
why: i was fascinated by how aerospace and automotive parts end up with those crazy organic shapes and wanted to understand the actual math instead of just clicking “optimize” in a black-box cad tool. building the whole thing from scratch forced me to internalize the compliance minimization, sensitivity filtering, and optimality criteria algorithms.
learned: i learned the full simp pipeline—how the power-law penalization forces intermediate densities toward solid or void, how sensitivity filters kill checkerboarding, and how the optimality criteria method with lagrange multipliers actually updates the densities each iteration. sparse matrix handling and modular code architecture (mesh, fem solver, filters, optimizer as separate layers) also became much clearer.
challenges: convergence could be finicky; small changes in filter radius or penalization power would either slow things down dramatically or produce checkerboard artifacts. making the live visualization update smoothly while the solver ran, and keeping the code modular enough that i could swap boundary conditions or load cases without rewriting everything, took several redesign passes.

title: fea playground 2D
description: an browser-native computational mechanics suite built to model, solve, and visualize 2D elastic truss and frame structures in real time
techSpecs: developed a computational mechanics suite for truss and frame analysis. i refactored the event loop and decoupled solvers from the rendering pipeline to eliminate lag.
why: i got tired of waiting for commercial fea packages or having to install heavy tools just to play with simple structural problems. i wanted a lightweight, interactive playground i could open in any browser and use to rapidly test ideas or verify hand calculations.
learned: i learned how to assemble global stiffness matrices from scratch, apply boundary conditions through static condensation, and solve the resulting linear systems efficiently enough for real-time browser use. mapping classical structural mechanics equations directly onto a hardware-accelerated rendering loop taught me a lot about performance trade-offs and numerical accuracy in javascript.
challenges: getting the stiffness matrix assembly and solver stable across different mesh densities was harder than expected. floating-point precision and making sure results matched analytical benchmarks (i checked against known cases and commercial software) took a lot of careful debugging. keeping the ui responsive while still solving the system on every parameter change was another constant balancing act.

title: 2R planar robot paddle
tag: physical automated robotic arm using inverse kinematics
description: mechatronics 2R planar arm playing a game similar to air hockey or pong, programmed in native python
techSpecs: created a mechatronics model using a trigonometric inverse kinematics (ik) solver. this maps 2d coordinates to joint angles in real-time with minimal latency
why: it was the first real hands-on mechatronics project that let me take pure textbook control theory and actually make something move and interact with the physical world. i wanted to prove i could close the loop from camera pixels → kinematics → motor torque on real hardware instead of just simulating everything.
learned: i learned how messy the gap is between ideal inverse dynamics and real motors. camera latency, non-uniform friction on the board, and the fact that simplified constant-inertia models sometimes outperformed the “full” textbook version on our small arm were big eye-openers. also got solid practice with opencv color tracking, forward kinematics for overlay visualization, and tuning pid gains until the arm stopped oscillating or going rigid.
challenges: the biggest ones were hardware-related: the cheap overhead camera introduced noticeable lag, so the predicted trajectory was always slightly behind reality. the ball would sometimes lose energy on wall bounces or get stuck in the middle despite the table tilt. gain tuning was also brutal—too much proportional gain and it overshot wildly, too much derivative and it became too stiff to hit fast balls. coordinating with the group on mechanical design while owning most of the software was another balancing act.

title: mechgenpro engine
tag: procedural kinematics engine that generates, simulates, and optimizes linkages
description: built a real-time procedural kinematics engine from scratch in lua + löve2d to figure out how planar mechanism synthesis and grashof classification actually work
techSpecs: architected a modular four-bar solver with forward kinematics, velocity/acceleration analysis, and a genetic optimizer for path matching. implemented custom vector math, newton-raphson solvers, and interactive trajectory tracing.
why: i wanted a fast, visual playground for mechanism design where i could generate valid linkages on the fly, watch their coupler curves, and optimize them — something more interactive than static textbook diagrams or heavy cad tools. it also let me explore procedural generation applied to mechanical systems.
learned: i got much more comfortable with the grashof criteria, transmission angles, four-bar position analysis, and numerical methods for solving linkage kinematics. building the generator + validator + optimizer loop taught me a lot about constraint handling and multi-objective design in mechanism synthesis. working in lua/löve2d was also a fun change of pace from the c++/python stack.
challenges: generating only valid, non-locking mechanisms while still exploring a useful design space required careful rule design. keeping the real-time animation smooth while doing continuous kinematic solves and optimization, and making the inspector ui feel responsive for live parameter tweaking, both needed iteration. avoiding singularities and making the optimizer produce mechanisms that actually move nicely (good transmission angles, smooth paths) was harder than the pure math suggested.

title: vehicle dynamics sim
description: real-time multi-body vehicle simulator with nonlinear tire physics, active controllers, and genetic algorithm suspension optimization
techSpecs: built a 14-DOF C++ vehicle dynamics engine with real-time RK4 integration, Pacejka Magic Formula tires, OpenMP parallelization, ABS/ESC systems, and GA-based suspension tuning.
why: i’ve always been interested in how cars actually behave at the limit — understeer, oversteer, load transfer, tire slip. i wanted to go beyond simple bicycle models and build something that could capture real handling metrics and let me experiment with control systems (abs/esc) and setup optimization in a high-fidelity environment.
learned: i learned a ton about multi-body vehicle modeling, nonlinear tire force generation with the magic formula, how suspension and aero interact with chassis motion, and the practical side of running stable real-time integration on a complex system. parallelizing the tire and suspension calculations with openmp and wiring up a genetic algorithm for multi-objective setup tuning were especially educational.
challenges: keeping a 14-dof system numerically stable at 1 ms timesteps while still running fast enough for interactive use was a major challenge. the pacejka model has a lot of parameters and can produce weird force curves if you’re not careful. coordinating the abs and esc logic so they don’t fight each other, and making the genetic algorithm converge on useful suspension setups without getting stuck in local minima, both took significant debugging and tuning.

title: PID control sim
description: interactive PID controller simulator for robotic and motor control systems with real-time response visualization engineered in c++
techSpecs: implemented a discrete-time pid algorithm for motor response modeling. the engine allows for live tuning of proportional, integral, and derivative parameters to visualize system damping.
why: after tuning pid gains on the physical 2r arm and seeing how sensitive real systems are, i wanted a clean, fast sandbox where i could experiment with classical control theory without hardware risk. it also felt like a natural bridge between pure theory and the kind of control code you eventually put on embedded systems.
learned: i deepened my understanding of anti-windup, derivative filtering, and how different plant dynamics (first-order vs second-order, with or without noise) completely change what “good” gains look like. building the metrics calculator and visualization pipeline forced me to think carefully about discrete-time integration and how to present control performance in a way that’s actually useful for tuning.
challenges: making the simulation feel interactive and responsive while staying numerically stable was harder than expected. some plant models would blow up or oscillate wildly with certain gain combinations, so i had to add safeguards and better default starting points. getting the performance metrics (especially settling time and overshoot) consistent across different reference signals also required careful definition and testing.

title: microgrid sim
tag: power electronics & MPPT microgrid simulator made in c++
description: high-fidelity c++ microgrid simulator featuring PV I-V curve modeling, adaptive MPPT control, DC-DC converter dynamics, and energy storage dispatch logic
techSpecs: built a high-fidelity pv simulator. it models i-v curves and uses an adaptive maximum power point tracking (mppt) algorithm to simulate converter responses to variable weather telemetry.
why: after building the higher-level python renewableenergysim, i wanted something lower-level and faster that could capture the actual power-electronics dynamics instead of just energy balance. i was curious how the control loops (especially mppt and dispatch) behave when you model the converters and battery physics more carefully, and c++ felt like the right tool for that kind of tight, real-time-ish simulation.
learned: i got a much clearer picture of how single-diode pv models respond to temperature and irradiance, how different mppt algorithms hunt for the maximum power point in practice, and how converter duty-cycle control and battery constraints interact during sudden changes in load or sunlight. designing a clean modular c++ architecture (models, controllers, utils) with proper interfaces also taught me a lot about keeping simulation code maintainable as it grows.
challenges: getting the i-v curve and mppt interaction numerically stable under rapidly changing conditions took iteration. balancing realism in the converter and battery models against simulation speed was constant. logging everything cleanly for post-analysis while keeping the core loop tight, and making sure the dispatch logic didn’t do something stupid (like over-discharging or fighting the mppt), required careful testing with different daily profiles.

title: renewable energy sim
tag: enterprise python renewable energy microgrid simulator
description: enterprise-grade python sim and interactive web dashboard for renewable energy microgrids using real-world weather data
techSpecs: designed an enterprise energy management simulator. it uses a modular dispatch algorithm to balance demand against storage, enabling sensitivity analysis on grid stability.
why: i wanted to explore the systems side of renewable energy—how generation, storage, and load actually interact under realistic weather conditions—rather than just looking at isolated component models. building something modular and dashboard-driven felt like a natural step toward larger energy-systems work.
learned: i learned the practical details of pv temperature derating, how a simple p&o mppt algorithm actually hunts for the maximum power point, battery soc integration with efficiency losses, and non-linear inverter efficiency curves. structuring a larger python project with clean separation (models, core engine, data fetchers, dashboard) was also valuable experience.
challenges: getting realistic weather data integration reliable (api rate limits, fallbacks to historical data) and making the load-balancing logic sensible under rapidly changing irradiance took time. keeping the simulation numerically stable over long time horizons while still being fast enough for interactive dashboard use was another balancing act.

title: robosim 3d arm simulator
tag: real-time inverse kinematics robotic arm simulation built with three.js
description: built a hardware-accelerated 3d robotic arm simulator from scratch in vanilla js + three.js to figure out how real-time inverse kinematics and multi-joint matrix transforms actually work
techSpecs: implemented a real-time ik solver that maps 3d target coordinates to joint angles, plus path caching, velocity telemetry, and hierarchical gripper transforms.
why: i wanted a pure software 3d counterpart to the physical 2r planar arm — something i could use to visualize and experiment with full inverse kinematics, hierarchical joint transforms, and tool-path behavior without needing hardware. building it in the browser with three.js also let me practice real-time 3d graphics and matrix math in a way that felt immediate and shareable.
learned: i got much deeper into 3d inverse kinematics (trig and matrix approaches for multi-joint arms), hierarchical scene graphs so rotations propagate correctly through parent-child joints, and how to keep a high-performance render loop while also running a secondary canvas for live telemetry graphs. path caching/playback and variable-speed execution taught me a lot about sequencing and time-scaling motion data.
challenges: getting the ik solver robust enough that the arm didn’t fold into weird configurations or lose solutions near singularities took iteration. keeping the 3d scene, the ik calculations, and the telemetry canvas all running smoothly at interactive frame rates required careful frame-loop design. making the gripper hierarchy and motion trails look clean without tanking performance, and balancing the “industrial automation” aesthetic with actual usability, were also ongoing refinements.

title: kinematicsJS
description: a fun, interactive engine to view kinematic and inverse kinematic data in real time
techSpecs: built an interactive engine for link dynamics. it uses a recursive matrix-based approach to compute forward and inverse kinematics at every frame for accurate positional visualization.
why: after working on the physical 2r arm i wanted a pure software sandbox where i could rapidly prototype different kinematic chains, test inverse-kinematics solvers, and visualize joint-space vs. task-space behavior without having to rebuild hardware every time.
learned: i deepened my understanding of transformation matrices, jacobian-based ik methods, and how to keep a real-time physics loop stable with collision resolution. building the visualization layer (charts, live joint angles, end-effector paths) also taught me a lot about clean interactive ui design for technical tools.
challenges: inverse kinematics singularities and making sure the solver stayed robust near them were tricky. balancing numerical stability of the physics integration with responsiveness in the browser, and keeping the code small enough to stay “compact” while still being useful, required careful trade-offs.
